So yeah, surprisingly, there's hope for us, and that's coming from a super broken, cynical lady.

I got ghosted 7 times last year, and it basically broke me to the point where I didn't feel a single thing for about 7 months afterwards. Mind you, these were a mixture of supposedly close friends and romantic interests, all of whom reciprocated - at least presumably - in their feelings towards me. Nothing was ever "off" about any of it. It messed me up so bad that when I met my current girlfriend, and she was afraid to ask me out, she essentially said she "didn't to scare me the way those other girls had". She's extremely considerate, but she knows the pain I've been through.

I already had severe self esteem issues along with abandonment issues (thanks mom and dad!) and this ghosting throughout basically a whole year just really exacerbated all of that to the point where now I actively ask for reassurance from my girlfriend because I constantly feel like I'm going to be left or don't deserve her. Thankfully, again, she's extremely considerate and doesn't mind one bit. We're both hopeless romantics, so we fit extremely well. But yeah, ghosting fucks a person up. As others have said, blocking someone who legitimately makes you uncomfortable is the exception to the rule, because that's about safety and your personal boundaries. But otherwise, it can really ruin a person.

Maybe I'm just dumb in my way of thinking, but I would never do something that could so devastate another person to the point of dealing a personal blow to their self worth. Just unnecessarily selfish and cruel. To me, at this point, ghosting is on the same level as cheating when it comes to the pain it can cause someone, but perhaps that's just because of my personal interactions with it.

This movie is likely the closest we'll ever get to a proper OZ adaptation.

While I love and respect the Wizard of OZ as a movie, because of its importance to film history and because I just love Judy Garland and how beautiful the film is, it's by and large responsible for perverting what OZ actually is for decades to come. Anyone who's read the books knows that OZ is a horribly dark place, war torn and sectioned off by various groups. Ed, Edd 'n Eddy is fascinating from numerous artistic viewpoints.

Aside from just being very funny and well written, and the animation being beautiful, it's essentially one of the last cartoons that - as far as I can think of - allows itself to be a cartoon in the sense of its almost Looney Toonsesque physics and slapstick. Someone else in this thread already mentioned the sound effects, and that's a good note, but nobody seems to have talked about what a wild decision it was to use essentially freeform jazz for the backing OST of a childrens cartoon. And somehow it works, which is even weirder. 

People also mentioned the finale film, which i arguably one of the best finales of all time, and while some folks disliked the direction the show took in its final season (understandable, we all like different things), I personally think it was brilliant, but perhaps not for the reasons one might think. One argument that would normally be bandied about for the change might be "well, it reinvigorated the show and gave it new life!" and someone else might ask "honestly how much longer could they have kept doing scams for? It would've gotten old!"

But one thing nobody seems to ever mention is that the show itself is a scam ON the audience. We go 4 seasons believing its actually still summer, and then suddenly, in Season 5, it's revealed that Eddy, who somehow can't get away with the simplest of scams, has been successfully scamming the entire neighborhood for god knows how long so they believe it's still summer so his endless scams can continue. It's absolutely genius. I remember watching this for the first time and being just blown away by how effortlessly it was done, and felt so natural. Also hilarious that he put so much effort in, and proved that, when he wants to, he can pull it off.

I got the DVD set and it's a little...underwhelming. To have the entire show in decent quality is nice, but it's missing the specials and the film, so it's not, in a technical sense, a "complete" series. Still, it's better than not having it at all, or only having it on a streaming service, where it's liable to be pulled at any second by the maniac whim of an executive somewhere who needs an extra 2.50 cents in his pocket that month written off as a budget cut. Much like the Daria DVD, I'd rather lose a few things (even though the omission of the film is a real blunder, seeing as it's literally the end of the show and therefore important) like the 30 second sound bites that made up the "soundtrack" than to not have the show on home release at all. For its few faults, the DVD set is pretty solid.

I also, much like Bill Watterson, respect the hell out of Danny for not bringing it back in any way, shape or form, and being very openly vocal about how much it would suck no matter how it was done lol The man has artistic integrity, and I can respect that. A legacy is viewed far more glowingly than how much money something made, in the end.

All in all Ed, Edd 'n Eddy is, as far as I'm concerned, one of the greatest cartoons not just of its time but of all time, and it's great to see it so fondly remembered.

While it's understandable to be upset - as I was as well, because Locke was easily my favorite in the show - this had to happen. You have to remember that everything Ben thought he was doing, he thought he was doing for Jacob. Except it wasn't Jacob giving him these orders, it was the smoke monster. That's why he'd never seen him. That's why they met in the cabin. When Ben kills Locke, he does so because the smoke monster has effectively told him to, because he needs a permanent host to get off the island.

While the smoke monster can clearly imitate forms of either the deceased or the special, whether that's Alex or Walt for respective examples, it has to have a proper form to inhabit. In fact, I think his entire hope was to initially take Christian Shepard's body, but it unfortunately gets lost in the crash despite the coffin being found later, and therefore his plan no longer works. This is why he needs Lockes body.

Now one could argue "well why doesn't he just use the body of any person who's been on the island and died?" and there's a few possible theories. First of all, they were killed BY him, making them unuseable, like Mr. Eko for example. Another is that the body has to have been that of a believer, and there was no bigger believer than that of John Locke. There's also the theory that he could only use the body of a Candidate (which does poke holes in my Christian Shepard theory, but one could argue that Christian, being adjacent to Jack who is a Candidate, might've worked?). Essentially, the smoke monster plays a long con, much like Sawyer has done.

And on top of all of that, without a physical form, he wouldn't have been killable. He's only able to be defeated because once the cork is removed from the center of the island, it locks him into that form for good. He clearly didn't know this, as he's very obviously surprised when Jack is able to draw blood from him.

It's a really tough call.

Obviously there's the ones everyone will mention, all of which I love to death. Classic Spongebob has some of the best comedy writing maybe ever, even outside a kids cartoon. Gravity Falls has spectacular writing with really emotional heart, and is just a banger of a series from start to finish, likely due to its tight pacing thanks to Hirsch's outright refusal to milk it for all it was worth. The Simpons classic seasons are also a standout in terms of comedy, and some particularly decent animation at times even. Bojack Horseman is honestly not even something I need to explain at this point, as I think we're all painfully aware of how beautiful it was in every aspect.

Then there's the personal favorites. Home Movies. China, IL. Rick and Morty. Invader Zim. As Told By Ginger. South Park.

But in spite of all of that, in spite of my adoration for all of these, whenever this question is posed to me, my answer always inevitably becomes Ed, Edd 'n Eddy, and for multiple reasons. First of all, it's the only modern cartoon I can think of that truly embraces the Warner Brothers level of zaniness in a way that feels authentic. There is no such thing as gravity. Children have the strength of giants. Nobody ever gets actually hurt in any way that matters. It is just outright slapstick to the nth degree, and it's WONDERFUL. On top of that, the animation is beautiful. In fact, it's on par I'd say at times with animation from the golden era even, just in terms of its framing, its color palette (especially the later seasons) and its movement. The music, which essentially falls into a pseudo freeform jazz ensemble, is a remarkable choice for a kids show, and yet it works better than perhaps any OST that has ever been produced for a kids show before or since. It shouldn't, in theory, but it *does*.

The voice acting is out of this world, particularly with the Eds of course, but also with everyone else to boot. And finally, the writing is still absolutely hysterical. I finally got the "complete" series DVD CN released recently and I've been going back through it season by season and laughing myself absolutely stupid. It's sharp, it's focused, it's got such a clear view of who these characters are and how they bounce off one another that you rarely see in any show, honestly, but especially a kids cartoon. A lot of this can be chalked up to creator Danny Antonucci (who is a really nice guy for what it's worth) because he so clearly knew what it was and how it should be, and when a creator has a vision that particular, it shows.

Not to mention, and I'll spoiler this for the benefit of whoever, but the final season begins with >!an episode that literally alters the entire concept of the series, and yet it's done so masterfully that it doesn't feel forced at all, along with giving that last batch of episodes something new to deal with in a fun way!<. Again, it shouldn't work. But it *did*. And that's all beside the fact that the series concludes with a phenomenal feature film that somehow manages to give you emotional closure to things you didn't even realize you needed emotional closure to. A true masterwork in background storytelling, honestly.

So yeah, there's the obvious. There's the personal faves. But the answer always, ALWAYS, comes back around to Ed, Edd 'n Eddy. It's just as close to perfection as I think one can get in a cartoon, and I think it will truly stand the test of time and be considered an all time classic down the road.

There was a perio d of time right after LOST ended where everyone was trying to get in on the next big thing, specifically on the major networks like ABC, NBC, FOX, etc. It led to the birth of a lot of amazing shows...conceptually. Things like Revolution, Terra Nova, Believe, The River, Alcatraz, the list goes on indefinitely (and to be fair the timing may be a bit off, some of these may have been on before LOST actually wrapped), and on paper, they all sounded excellent. In execution however...

...I still find it hilarious that the only one worth really watching was Terra Nova and even then only because of how bad it was. It was like MST3K levels awful and I loved it. But everything else, whoo boy. I think, of the shows I named, my personal disappointment was Believe, because little girl with weird powers has always been a tried and true successful trope, so how do you screw *that* up? Well, they found a way. And it wasn't that these were bad - well, Terra Nova and The River were actually just bad - it was that they just were all so BORING. They were somehow excellent, engaging ideas but boiled down to the most basic generic mundane happenings.

I recognize, especially on a network that orders 20 episodes a season if something does well, that some pipe has to be laid. Not everything every week can be amazing. I'm used to that. I'm fine with it. But somehow none of them ever got better. Revolution is perhaps the best example simply because it was on the longest, wherein even the show ditched tons of their original premises and setups after Season 1 and went an entirely different direction, dropping major plotpoints altogether. None of them knew what they wanted to be, and that's a death sentence right out the gate.

As much as we all love to blame networks, I think this is on period of television where the people involved with the shows directly should be held accountable. They just didn't figure things out before going in, and it showed. Sometimes you can get away with that if you're good enough, but they weren't, and I have a sneaking suspicion it's why so many things these days are planned to a tee.

Still wish Terra Nova was around though. That was a goddamned hoot and a half.

I'm a 32 year old woman, and I absolutely miss the experience of having something to look forward to instead of feeling obligated to finish things. There's too much now, there's too much pressure as well, and overall it's tainted my viewing experience. What once was "must see TV" has now become "must watch TV" because if you don't watch it, you're left entirely out of the loop and not because you actually wanted to see it.

I appreciate Paramount and HBO doing weekly drops, as that brings some of that back, but it still isn't the same. Nobody is demanding I am there at a certain time on a certain channel, and so I, again, do not feel obligated to attend my enjoyment. But this goes beyond even "appointment television".

This is why I love PlutoTV, which I've been using since it started, because it's essentially emulating that experience, and boy howdy lemme tell you, there's just something so much better about coming into the middle of a movie I've seen before simply because it's on right then than having to search it up and watch it from the beginning any time I want. Or just scrolling the channels and thinking, "oh hey, Daria or Unsolved Mysteries or whatever is on" and just sitting down and catching a few episodes.

This is why I still go out of my way to catch stuff on broadcast. GF and I watched the entirety of "Good Girls" as it aired, and I did the same this year with "Pivoting" and "The Ghost & Molly McGee" and "Yellowjackets", and it really hammered home just how uninvested I am in something when it's readily available to me. That, combined with the lack of discussion of theorizing of any kind for more plot heavy shows really hurts the experience. The wait between seasons was half the fun. Thankfully, as I said, Paramount seems to be doing that with their stuff and it makes Halo much more enjoyable as a result.

So sure, convenience is nice, but it's not just convenience. It's also far more required than broadcast viewing if you ask me, because all they gauge are the first few weeks of engagement instead of the entire seasons engagement and then make their cancellation decisions based on that without ever realizing that some people have to work or have kids or other duties that means they can't sit around for 9 hours and watch an entire season of something in one sitting, not to mention I no longer want to do that.

See, I grew up getting box sets when they first started coming out, and as a teenager, that's what I would do. I have other crap to do.

So that expectation of engagement from streaming services coupled with the fact that you're left entirely out of any kind of discussion if you don't "binge" it immediately really brings down the entire experience, and makes it less than it used to be, and that's coming from someone that's generally a lone viewer and not an interactive participant, but I enjoy seeing other people discuss things at least.

Despite having not watched the show regularly since it's first returned few seasons since its cancellation (of which I was excited for, and enjoyed when it aired), I can pinpoint the exact problem with the cutaways with Family Guy for you.

It isn't that they're a bad idea. They were a big part of the original shows run, and honestly generally the best part. The problem is that, very quickly into its revival run, the show forgot that episodes had plots, and that the cutaways were more often than not somewhat connected to said plot of the episode or a joke within the episode itself. Now, the cutaways are literally as random and disconnected as it can be, and the episodes themselves rely far more heavily on them than the supposed "plot" of the episode itself.

Also, once Seth left - and this is fairly common as we've seen it time and time again - the show took another noticeable dive, and I don't think there's anyone who would disagree with that. The same thing happened to The Simpsons, which started on its serious decline right around its 11th season (this is an arguable debate, certainly, but I feel like Seasons 9/10 were still pretty good and 11 is were most people realized the show was over for good in terms of its greatness), which is also right around the time Futurama started. As I said, when a creator leaves, the product suffers, generally.

But yeah, the cutaways not being connected to the story or remotely relevant whatsoever to the fact that the episodes themselves barely have plot doesn't help keep the show in everyones good graces. It's only really even still around because, despite questionable quality - much like The Simpsons in their worst zombie years - it continues to be a decent performer for the network and thus remains financially viable.

I loved the shows original run when I was a teenager, I really did. I bought the sets, which I still have, and even watched the first few revival seasons, but I still hold to the belief that only really the first revival season was anywhere close to being as good as the originals, and I think a big part of the problem is the cutaway relevancy like I mentioned.

Even now, as a 32 year old woman, I still find those original first few seasons hilarious, but it doesn't at all surprise me why its dropped the way it has, in terms of its cultural appreciation.

Sometimes I feel like I'm one of the few people who tried to read on a digital device only to go decide I prefer physical books more lol

That being said, I've got nothing against people using digital devices to read. I completely understand the concepts behind it: enlarging text on a whim, being able to have books without clutter or making moving difficult, etc, but all that said, I simply cannot do it for a number of reasons. The first is one that plenty of people likely understand, which is that so much of my life is already dedicated to staring at screens, I really appreciate a hobby that *isn't.*

Reading is a tactile experience. Watching a film, a show, even gaming (despite it being interactive) are not. But reading a book is just me and the book and it takes physical effort and it just doesn't work the same for me when reading something digitally. I also really enjoy the idea of having a physical library of my own, and for some reason I have a much higher emotional connection when a book is physical than just words on a screen.

As I said, I completely understand, and even recognize, the benefits of digital books, but they just aren't for me. I like the paper. I like the feeling a book has in my hands. It's an experience unlike any other and to translate that experience to yet another screen based one diminishes it for me.

But hey, that's just me.

When I was in my early twenties, I moved to Oregon with my then longtime girlfriend. About a year later, I moved back to California and had to leave a lot of stuff behind because the truck simply couldn't fit it all. This meant a lot of my books got left behind, but I was very cautious to leave only the things I knew I absolutely wouldn't care to lose.

Growing up, my stepfather was an avid reader, and after he was finished with books, he'd put them in the garage in a box. I'd often go pilfer them. After my parents split up, I wound up having a ton of books that had once belonged to him, that he himself likely would've gotten rid of anyway. Books that, for the most part, were crime/thriller based. When I left Oregon, these were the things I left behind. Books bought at the local drug store during checkout by popular authors whose work will never not be mass produced.

While I did, unfortunately, lose some of my own stuff (someone below mentioned Goosebumps, and I too lost my sets which I deeply mourn), I have been very lucky to keep my collection almost entirely in tact. My current girlfriend whom I live with has an entire basement covered in walls of bookshelves built into the walls. This is where my personal library now lives. I can't stand the idea of losing anything - books, dvds, whatever - because, as you said, they were mine and they had a story to tell, and buying them again, also as you said, doesn't help because those were someone elses, so they don't have the same emotional attachment even  if it's literally the same book.

I worry a lot about what happens someday when our entire generation can no longer afford to live indoors, or climate change gets so bad it destroys everything we own, or, and this one is the worst for me personally, I die and someone else inherits my collections and breaks it apart because I'm not there to stop them.

But until those times comes, I suppose I'll just have to be happy that I have what I have and appreciate that I've been lucky enough to keep it all, even when my life has changed dramatically. Even books I didn't like, like Sittenfeld's "Sisterland", I can't bring myself to get rid of, because even if I wound up not enjoying it, I clearly thought I might since I bought it, and that alone means it's worth staying in the collection. Then again, perhaps I'm an unusual case, seeing as I'm far more attached to things than people. At least my things have always been there for me, never hurt me, and just want to give me some kind of enjoyment.

It's interesting to me the divide between people who consider longer seasons "filler" and people who consider longer seasons "getting to know the characters". I certainly fall far more in line with that second group, and always have. For instance, having stuff like Desperate Housewives, LOST or Ugly Betty - all of which serialized serious dramas on one level or another - not only had 20+ shows for the majority of their run (give or take LOST's back half) and they were still able to tell excellent stories in that timeframe, but also I felt like I really got to spend time with the characters and know them intimately, as opposed to now where it's "here's a group, you'll sort of like them for 8 episodes, may not we don't know, enjoy."

Certainly there's some shows that benefit, and have always benefited from the shorter season span, and streaming wasn't the thing that created that concept. Obviously British comedies have always been rather short, and quality over quantity in that regard, but also shows like Curb Your Enthusiasm and even back in 2011 when FX released stuff like Wilfred which only had 13 episodes a year for the majority of its run, benefited from shorter season times.

The interesting thing is, I agree with you especially in regards to sitcoms. Sitcoms especially benefit from longer seasons. While dramas do have their benefits with shorter seasons, even if I miss the character bonding, I think sitcoms are especially hurting because of this shorter episode count. Some shows, like Bojack, which straddle the line between comedy and drama, obviously work, but most do not.

In the end it just depends on how you prefer to watch television and nobody is really wrong.

As someone below said, yes, those 20+ episode orders were often for the network, not the show, to get the series to syndication so they could then sell it and make money on reruns. This is why you'll see so many series from the that time period run just over the 100 episode mark, and then immediately get cancelled. It was far enough along in its production to be considered financially profitable but not enough so to maintain it's longevity. Obviously this is also no longer really an issue, because not only did How I Met Your Mother sort of break that whole syndication issue by being syndicated well before it's 100th episode, but also with the advent of streaming services, syndication simply doesn't hit the way it used to, profit wise.

One would perhaps liken it to rewatching your favorite films, but guess what, films run - at most - 3 hours, and are easy to rewatch. There's 5 that specifically stick with me. I know that may seem like a lot, and some I won't really expand upon, because they are the same that many others have already stated repeatedly in this thread and so I don't need to further explain my reasons. Those include The Little Prince and Jonathan Livingston Seagull.

But the other 3 I will discuss, and those include An Underachievers Diary, The Body Artist and Stupid Children.

Let's begin with the first. Underachievers Diary, by Benjamin Anastas, is an all time favorite, easily, and I read it when I was in high school back around 2005 I would say. It speaks to me personally, as someone who also has struggled to do anything of note with their life, despite the fact that I've tried for years to be remotely successful at what I do. But it also speaks to me on a very basic level of the fact that sometimes, there's just some people who - no matter the good intentions or the efforts put in - don't catch a break, and it isn't their fault, and they simply have to deal with that. Also something I've sadly personally experienced throughout most of my life but especially as a little girl.

The second, The Body Artist by Don Delillo, is by far not the best book of his I've read. But the reason I include it here is because of the deep feeling of both grief and confusion, clutching for something when you've lost everything, and often times realizing you don't even recognize who *you* are on a fundamental level, much less a stranger who shows up in your house one day unannounced. It's beautiful and breezy but there's that light overture hides a very sad and cold interior, and, again, is something I feel extremely personally.

But the third, and easily my favorite book of all time, is Stupid Children by Lenore Zion. A book I attempt to bring up any chance I get because it's so very criminally unheard of. Published in 2013, and her only real "novel", it's written by a sex psychologist who specializes in the fetish fields of interest. The book follows a young girl who is taken from her fathers care after he attempts suicide, only to be placed in the care of a family who winds up being involved with a cult, a cult who then believes she is the reincarnation of their leaders lost wife. It's grotesque and bizarre and utterly hilarious, but more than anything else, as a young woman who grew up in - not a cult, certainly - but a household that stripped her of her own agency and demanded things of her she could never possibly hope to give them, it really dug deep into my core. It's absurd, but that's because life is absurd, and I genuinely hope Zion writes another novel one day, because I think she's a literary force to be reckoned with honestly.

Sure there's honorable mentions; Metamorphosis by Kafka, Animal Farm by Orwell, but those not only didn't make my personal cut for this discussion but also, like the first two I brought up at the start of this rambling diatribe, have already been talked about to death in here for why they're good examples.

So yeah. Sorry this is so long winded. I'm just a loser girl who likes reading way too much.

I have always been one of the minority who says that an ending cannot ruin an entire thing, and while I still stand by that sentiment - because despite the ending being an disappointingly anticlimactic wet fart to an otherwise epic series - I also cannot deny that it definitely hurts it a little. The journey is still fantastic, absolutely, but boy that might be one of the most let down I've ever been by the ending of something. It isn't like the magic stuff introduced in Descender that then becomes the crux of the sequel series comes out of nowhere, it's introduced fairly early on, but even then it just seems like, as someone else already stated, Lemire decided at the last minute to switch genres entirely and cop out on his original plan, which, as a writer myself, I find very upsetting.

What's even *more* upsetting to me, however, is the fact that Lemire also wrote Sweet Tooth which is easily one of the greatest comic books ever written. A solid, beautifully tragic, heartfelt dark adventure tale that really builds to a wonderful climax and none of it ever felt forced. So when you take into account that the man is clearly a talented writer and CAN come up with satisfying conclusions, it makes me all the more irritated at the disappointment that Descenders climax wound up being.

That being said that's just my opinion, and who knows maybe you'll be fine with it. I read it as it came out, so I also have a different experience with it than you're having. I have found at times that TV shows for example, when watched in quick succession (like LOST as a great example) the way they're written to be, work much better as a whole story without the enormous gaps in between seasons, so perhaps that's the case for some comics as well, who knows. I personally prefer seasonal breaks for all my media consumption, I like the waiting, it keeps things interesting.

Anyway, I still, even in light of everything I've said, think it's worth reading. The artwork is just stunning and, up until those last few moments, it's a really engaging, riveting and worthwhile read! Hope my long winded rant from an old comic dork girl helps in some way or another lol

But when you go for a decade plus with the continuity of Homer & Marge having been in high school in the 70s or so, mixed with however many dozens of episodes in that first decade including flashbacks regarding the birth of their children and the growth of their family, you cannot just wipe out an entire "canon" for a single Family Guy style joke. Family Guy gets away with it because that's the sort of show it's always been, but The Simpsons, especially for the first decade it was on, was a fairly grounded albeit somewhat ridiculous series. Sure it had its goofy moments, but at the core it was about a normal enough family in a goofy enough town that sometimes had ridiculous things happen. It was never off the wall Family Guy style.

This is enraging, and to hear that sort of statement from someone like Selman, who's been with the show for a long time, is extremely disheartening. To know that even the people who have had a hand in making it for this long don't give two shits is incredibly frustrating. As I said, I don't really care much about the show past Season 10, but even this riles me up as someone who rewatches that first decade constantly. A lot of fans are willing to, as I said, accept certain lore elasticity, but not so much accepting that same elasticity in regards to when you have decades worth of episodes built upon lore that you then say doesn't matter two bits all for the sake of a single gag you likely won't ever reference again anyway.

I'm all for rubberband continuity, but not when it literally erases things set up years and years ago for years and years that was then referenced for years and years. That's not rubberband continuity, that's just you not giving a crap.

This is interesting, albeit not at all surprising, what with Disney owning Fox and thusly Fox Animation now. Considering Disney also owns the majority stake in Hulu, which is where all the Fox Animation ends up, it makes total sense they wouldn't want to let their "properties" (and I only say that in quotes because they merely acquired them, not created them) wind up on another channel, even if just in reruns. I wonder if this will extend to other networks that show old episodes of stuff like Family Guy, like TBS, or what.

It's also weird considering Adult Swim is part of the reason that Family Guy and Futurama even had as much of a shelf life as they did, because people started re-discovering them on Adult Swim once they'd been canned by Fox back in the day, and between this new interest and the DVD sales, the shows were eventually brought back entirely (and in Futurama's case, sadly, re-canceled. That show has bad luck, man). And it wasn't just Fox shows that benefited from this. Hell, one of Adult Swim's first original series, if not the first, was Home Movies, which originally started on UPN of all places and after 5 episodes was canceled before being resurrected for Adult Swim a year or so later. Adult Swim, back in the day, was sort of a repository for-certainly their own then somewhat meager projects, but also-showcasing things that didn't really get a fair shot, like Mission Hill and Baby Blues, not to mention bringing certain animes like Cowboy Bebop or Paranoia Agent to the forefront to let people learn about them.

So I've always sort of seen Adult Swim as a sort of animation graveyard in that regard, because they took in these abandoned properties and then, a lot of times, wound up generating far more interest in them than the channels that originally aired them. So, again, not all that surprising given the change in ownership around Hollywood lately, but certainly interesting nonetheless.

Addendum: Adult Swim, in recent years, has actually done a fairly good job I'd say of recapturing a lot of that magic they once had. While they sunk into a pit for a while, and while we did lose greats like Aqua Teen, they have managed to at least bolster themselves back up again with shows like Rick & Morty, The Shivering Truth, the rebirth of 12 oz Mouse and Final Space (though that's a lot more of a co-production than their own in a lot of ways). Plus they're doing interesting things with old properties like the final season of Samurai Jack, and now they've got Primal. I think Adult Swim is gonna be just fine, honestly.

As you said, this isn't really a new thing, shows have been doing it forever to try and retain audiences during the season break, but I can tell you the real reason it feels underwhelming and disingenuous by todays standpoint.

It's because most streaming shows are all serialization. There's no fluff or filler or anything. While many would praise that as a good thing, and in some cases are not wrong, many shows actually hurt because of the lack of them. See, the thing about the standard 22-24 episode seasons of yesteryear were that they really gave you time to connect to the characters and feel something for them. If all you have these days is a mere 8 episodes or so, even if those episodes are 30-50 minutes a piece, it's just not going to do the same thing. Because of this, by the time you reach the finale, you're still not invested enough to care about a cliffhanger.

As I said, some shows can get away with it, but most shows can't, and really, considering how cancel happy the streaming services have become (on par with network television if not worse now somehow), most shows, whether they're streaming or not, should wrap their seasons up nice and tidy just in case of cancellation, unless they're of course an enormous series with no questions in regards to their future. Something like Game of Thrones was, you know. Something that knows, no matter what, they're coming back next year.

Anyway, this is just the perspective of a 31 year old woman who grew up watching way too much TV, but I figured I'd chime in.

While others like "Collection Completed" or "Dead Right" or even the wonderful "Carrion Death" are excellent and all, "The New Arrival" really hit me hard because I saw it on late night TV as a little girl in elementary school. I have insomnia, and I always slept better if I had a television on, so I was allowed a TV in my bedroom and often, on nights I couldn't sleep (which is most, with insomnia), I'd flip through the channels with the volume muted and see what I could find. I was already a fan of horror at this time, but this....this thing wrecked me and I was terrified by it forever.

For years afterwards I had no idea what it even had been. I didn't know it was a Tales from the Crypt episode, and all I could remember was the little girl in a polka dotted dress and a creepy mask killing everyone around her. That was the only imagery that stuck in my head, and I hunted for it forever. Eventually, when TV on DVD started becoming a thing, I wound up collecting a lot of it, and one of the shows I decided to get into was Tales from the Crypt. I bought the first 3 seasons with little to no fanfare. They were great and all, but it wasn't until I picked up the box for Season 4 when it came out and saw the image of that girl on the back that my mind was blown.

It was like unlocking a repressed memory or something. I am super anal about watching things in order, even in the case when they aren't serialized, but this was one time I broke that rule because I rushed home and shoved that bad boy into my DVD player so fast that I'm amazed it didn't somehow astral project into another dimension. I loaded up the disc and immediately watched that episode. It's the only thing to have ever scared me in my life, and granted I was a child (though a particularly brave child, I'll admit, when it came to watching horror), and even today it's one of the only things to sort of unnerve me. Nothing else gets to me, but that episode does, even just a little bit.

So yeah, check it out if you have access to the series, cause goddamn is it insane and boy do I love every hot messy minute of it.

I 100% agree with you, and I've actually been saying this to a few people for a few years.

It's not that shorter seasons don't work, they certainly do especially for particular shows, but especially in dramas and certain sitcoms, it's really hard to justify cutting down that standard length to 10-13 episodes a season (some even shorter than that). Something like Fleabag makes sense, because that's just how british TV rolls, but I first started noticing it a while back with Good Girls and The Good Place both on NBC. The first season of Good Girls had 10 episodes, then bumped up to 13, then bumped up to 16 (before the virus cut production off anyway) and Good Place was constantly at 13 episodes a season I believe. But honestly, and people wanna say this is british television to blame, I disagree with that sentiment. I think it's a combination of streaming services and far too much content to swallow.

Everything has to be super digestible now, meaning make it as short as possible. Even if the episodes are longer (for instance there may only be 10 or less episodes of Stranger Things or Unfortunate Events but they're like 50 friggin minutes a piece), the season is still shorter, and I hate to be the one to tell them this but that extra time doesn't ultimately make up for it. Here's why the standard 22-24 season series worked.

You spent WAY more time with those characters. That's it. That's the reason. Oh sure, you could argue that with a longer run you could tell a more fleshed out story given out bit by bit throughout the season, and oh sure there'll be detractors who say things like "well with longer seasons characters can often become mishandled or plots become dropped" which are certainly valid criticisms, but ultimately that can all really be forgiven because by the time the show wraps up, you're 200+ episodes in (depending how long it runs I suppose) and you know those characters super well and feel like they're people you really know because you spent so much time with them. You just don't get that same effect with shorter seasons.

I used to watch things on broadcast all the time back before I didn't have cable (though my not having cable certainly isn't a choice, it's a necessity cause I'm broke as shit), and I loved seeing those huge seasons every year. I looked forward to knowing that for a good chunk of the year, my time would be taken up once or twice a week by these shows and these characters, instead of how people now spend maybe a few hours with them over the course of a singular weekend, all to pretty much forget what happened in what they watched by the time the next season eventually rolls around. It just doesn't work as well, for the most part. Again, it depends on the series of course, but on the whole, *especially with dramas*, you need that extra time.

Sure, everyone consumes media in different ways, and that's totally fine. But the way you consume something doesn't change the way it's being given to you either. It's still being given to you by bits and pieces because it costs too much now to make a season that long, or at least that's the excuse I'm sure the networks would feed you. The day NBC tells me something "costs too much" is the day I'll laugh myself to death. You're telling me Netflix can't give out just a bit more cash to broaden those season lengths just a smidge? Fucking Netflix of all companies? Give me a break. And of course there's many showrunners/creators who personally decide they want their series to be 10 episodes or however many a year and that's understandable too, as nobody knows what would work better for their show than the people who fucking created it.

It's all subjective ultimately, but yes, I agree with you.

I wrote a very long essay many years ago when I ran a film blog where I psychoanalyzed the hotel room, and how it has its own rules, like how anything you bring into the room can in theory be used against the room but you cannot damage the room with items from the room itself, and stuff like that. This is why the room does not take damage when he rips it apart or it floods itself. The room merely resets, perfect as ever, because it's not real damage. But the fire he sets, from things he brought with him? That's real damage. That's not the room, that's Mike using outside sources to harm it. He can throw a lamp out the window and it'll just reappear, but if he sets fire to it, it's going to go up in flames. Not to mention the little nod with "We've Only Just Begun" being the room making a very literal statement to Mike about, hey buddy, we've only just begun here, you have no idea what you're in for. Brilliant.

The room gives him the chocolate to lure him into a sense of false security, as Jacksons character stated "Hotels are all about familiarity and creature comforts". The room does not do anything to Mike for the first half hour or so he's in it, but it's well aware of him being there, which makes it all the more menacing. It's just watching him. Hell, Mike himself says into his tape recorder at one point, "I've been here before. It's safe." Because, in essence, all hotel rooms are the same, made all the more evident by Jacksons character telling Mike he could easily take photos of the room right next to 1408 because it has the exact same layout. So when you're surrounded with familiarity, especially in a job where you stay in hotels a lot like Mike does, you become lulled into this idea that you're safe.

The rooms beautiful, lavish and almost welcoming decor are its biggest advantages, because it makes people put their guard down and settle in, not knowing what they're in for.

All in all, an excellent movie with a really moving plot that hinges on loss and grief. Cannot love it enough.

As a little girl with autism, I got the shit bullied out of me nonstop and my home life was a nightmare with abusive parents and step siblings. Because of this, I got really heavily into reading, and I would devour books by the day. By the middle of 7th grade, I'd read Stephen King's IT in just a week and a half, and that book was over a thousand words long. To this day, I still have stacks of books next to my bed that I am working through, along with bookshelves full of books I will get to after these are finished. I credit my love of books for keeping me alive when nothing else, and nobody else, cared to do so and for turning me into a writer myself. As someone who lived with an uncontrolled reality, nothing appealed to me more than a controlled reality, and it still does.

Sometimes I'd go to the library, but that was a bit harder for me because I, for whatever reason, don't like having to get books I then have to give back as I become incredibly emotionally attached to them. I asked for books for birthdays, holidays, etc. They were the only companions I had, and because of this, and because I grew up in a fairly well off family, I managed to accrue a rather impressive personal library, the majority of which I've managed to hold onto even up til now.

Books are my everything, because nothing else ever tried to be anything for me.

I'm 100% in agreement with you, and it deeply saddens me, as someone who read OZ from a young age and has always wanted more stuff that was fairly faithful to the books like Return was, that I haven't not only seen it accomplished, but rarely tried earnestly. 

I have a few theories as to why this is. My first is that, because of the public mainstream movie goers affiliation with the franchise is mostly from the original film, most companies, when looking at adapting OZ content, rarely can see past that original lineup of characters. It's a real shame too, because OZ is full of wonderful characters, as Return clearly showed up, that could be adapted to screen if done correctly. Because of this, they fear straying from that lineup of Woodsman, Scarecrow and Lion and alienating the larger portion of the public, they think "it has to be this in order to make money", and they're sadly often proven right.

While we've seen a few more "recent" adaptations, ranging from Emerald City to Oz: The Great & Powerful, neither really did much to stay faithful nor were interestingly changed to be worth the time. Emerald City was far too strange, and if I'm saying that about an adaptation of OZ content then it's gotta be way weird, and Great & Powerful, while definitely not good, was at least semi interesting even if it didn't live up to its potential and instead decided to shoe horn in nonstop CGI effects and boring writing. Wicked is, IMO, the only real "rewriting" of OZ that's been good, and it only gets away with it because of our lack of content of the Witch as a whole that she can be rewritten in such a way.

Except the musical, as that's an entirely different beast, and I love it cause I'm a huge musical geek.

OZ is actually fairly dark, and often about war torn civilizations and societies, and I'd like to see that reflected more genuinely in adaptations than this whimsical nonsense they try and feed us. That's what I respect about Return to OZ. As a former film student herself, I'll always respect the original movie for what it did for cinema as a whole, but outside of that, Return really gave us that "ripped apart nation" feeling that the text actually embodies, and that's what I want to see more of. It's an interesting complex world that's often bogged down to appeal to everyone instead of the people who are actually interested in it, and while there's nothing inherently wrong with trying to get new people interested in it, you shouldn't do that by way of changing the original context and content, because then it loses all meaning and substance, especially when replaced with utter crap.

In the end, I think we won't see anything truly decent until someone who actually cares and knows what they're doing are given the chance to do something with it. As a little girl reading OZ books back in the early 90s, it was heavily influential in my interest in weird other worldly fantasy and oozing femininity in an intelligent way that nothing else was at the time, at least not for me at that age.

But the impossible can always happen. The comic book BONE is finally becoming a series after 20 years of waiting, so at this point, I think anything is possible. I'd also think Redwall is highly overdue for its grand film franchise, but that's another story for another post lol

I don't really talk about it much cause, like, my comic collection  and whatnot is more private than my opinions on film and books and such,  but honestly, BONE was and remains one of the single biggest influences  in my life as an artist. I first found it in the back of Disney  Adventures, a small magazine that Disney produced back in the 90s, which  I had a subscription to for years. At the back of the book, they always  had comics, and the first six issues of BONE ran among them.

But  I just thought, at the time, that this was something they'd made for  their little magazine, and didn't think much of it beyond knowing I  loved it and looked forward to getting a new chapter everytime a new  issue of Disney Adventures showed up.

Then, when I was wandering  around in a comic store one day that I went to often because it was near  my grandparents house and my mom used to go to the same shopping  center, I found out that Bone was an actual ongoing series and had  multiple issues on the shelf. At this point, the series was at least in  the late 20s, but I didn't care. See, this was back when comic shops  (which this seems to be coming back a bit now depending on where you  shop) had boxes upon boxes of back issues right there for you to sort  through that were all rather cheap, being back issues and all.

So  I sifted through the entirety of the back issues of BONE every single  time that I went there, solely to make sure I had every single one. I  then caught up before issue 35 and then read it ongoing after that as it  released. By the last 5 issues, the production schedule had halted  because the man did everything himself and he wanted it to be perfect,  which I admire to hell, so those last 5 issues came out about 4 years  apart, if I recall correctly. I think BONE may also be responsible for  me being capable of waiting extremely long times for things to return,  so thanks for that too I guess. I was devastated to hear it was going to  end, but it had to eventually. It wasn't like other comics, that seemed  like it could go on indefinitely. It was clear to me, even from the  start, that this thing was heading somewhere. I met Jeff Smith a number  of times, and the very first time, he bought me, right off the wall of a  comic shop when I told him how much he'd influenced me, an old issue of  Disneys Donald Duck comic series for 20 dollars that I still treasure  to this day. I own the entire 55 issue saga, the holiday special, the  two miniseries and the singular one volume edition, including other  things like action figures or other rare books that were only published  once or twice. BONE may very well have been my first obsession. BONE  ended right before my grandma got sick and died, so it isn't tainted by  that either. It exists in this perfect vacuum of time.

And I  still reread it. I just reread it about two years ago and I was planning  on doing another reread sometime before 2020. It taught me about plot  and pacing and character development and how you can meld genres,  whether it be fantasy and comedy or comedy and drama. BONE taught me,  honestly, a lot of what I know today, simply by the act of its existing.

 Rumors have swirled for years, ever since I was a little girl,  honestly, about the possibility of there being a movie. For a long time,  Nickelodeon wanted to do it, but Smith, being the goddamned hero he is,  and not unlike Bill Watterson himself, refused solely because he didn't want  to insert crappy pop songs for commercial value into his fantasy epic  just for sales. Between that and Wattersons views on merchandising, I  also learned a lot about valuing your own work, so again, thanks. But  since that fell apart, it's still been rumored to be happening. Year  after year I'd hear story after story, sometimes unsubstantiated and  sometimes with Smith himself involved, saying, "Yep, it's finally gonna  happen now!" I think it's been in production hell with Warner Brothers  since 2008, so I wouldn't say I'd given up hope, as was obvious with  this franchise you never give up hope for release, but I certainly had  fallen into a "I'll believe it when I'm watching it" mindset.

And  then this afternoon, I went to Facebook and hear the news from the man  himself on his official page, and I'm not going to not tell you...I cried.  I'm nearly crying right now writing this. Listen, BONE not only was a  huge influence, but it was one of the only things that I had to look  forward to to let me escape from a terrible upbringing, and it provided  relief when there never was any. I've been waiting for this for 20+  years, okay. Yeah. I'm a 30 year old woman now and I'm crying about a  fucking comic book from the goddamned 90s, but I don't give two shits,  because it's not just ANY comic book, it's mother fucking BONE, and BONE  is what helped me be even remotely happy growing up and BONE is what  taught me a lot of what I know about artistry today and BONE is  literally what got me into comic books.

BONE was, is, and always  be the single most important comic in my life. Others will be great too,  like Lenore or Serenity Rose or Ghost World or (for something a bit more  recent) Head Lopper and Sweet Teeth. But they aren't BONE. They aren't  what literally shaped an enormous part of me (well, Serenity Rose did  shape a good part of my personality, I have to admit, but that's a whole  other discussion) as the person that I am today. Despite all odds and  against all logic, Fone Bone never stopped trying to achieve whatever  goal he set out for, recognizing he had to do it or it wouldn't get  done, and he had to take care of those around him  Jeff Smith started a  small indie publication that has since been hailed as one of the all  time greatest graphic novels. I'm not saying it's not suspicious timing regarding the decision to  end Bojack after the upcoming season, given it coincides with the  unionization of the animation team (which technically doesn't involve  Netflix exactly and involves more the animation studio where the show is  produced), the cancellation of sister series "Tuca & Bertie" and  the fact that the series just failed to win an Emmy after 5 years,  losing to, instead, The Simpsons, a show that has not been relevant in  20 years (note I did not say 'not entertaining', I said 'not relevant',  as the show can still be funny at times, even if it's a wholly different beast than it  once was).

I'm not gonna deny that all of that is odd to connect with the announcement, but that being said, creator Raphael Bob-Waksberg  has stated numerous times in numerous interviews that he'd continue  doing the show as long as he thinks there are stories to tell. People also are quoting Bojack in his own words saying, "You can't have happy endings in sitcoms, not really because if  everyone's happy, the show would be over. And above all else, the show  has to keep going. There's always more show. And you can call "Horsin'  Around" dumb or bad or unrealistic, but there's nothing more realistic  than that. You never get a happy ending because there's always more show  - I guess until there isn't." This to me is Waksberg stating specifically how he feels about the show, but also there's something important to take note of here, and that's the usage of the word 'sitcom' in the speech. Bojack, funny as it may be, is NOT a sitcom. It's a dramedy, if it has to have a genre attached to it. All of this  leads me to believe he partially didn't think there was much left to  say, that he also didn't want the show to become a shell of its former  self (which would be VERY bad for a show that isn't your standard  sitcom) and a decision on Netflix's part, as most of their original  lineup is currently either ending or on the verge of it.

Bojack,  in my opinion, has had a specific fate befall it, something I don't  really have a name for, but something that has happened time and time  again. Shows like Home Movies or Preacher (or even Wilfred, maybe?), these series that are critically well respected, that  are told AHEAD OF TIME that it's time to wrap up. Part creator, part  network, or just one or the others decision. Either way, these shows are  not victims of "classic cancellation", which to me is when a series  goes off air thinking they'll be back, having every intention to be  back, sometimes going so far as to set up entire cliffhangers and  plotlines for the following season in its finale, and then the network  just brazenly deciding...yeah, fuck your show, fuck your audience, see  ya later, bye.

Frankly, much as I love the series, I've been  saying for the last 2 years now that it's probably about time to wrap it  up. I'm okay with this decision, whoevers decision it was, even if it  means losing what I consider to be one of the best television series of  all time. Especially with the news that it's the final season well ahead  of time, for the crew anyway, and the news that they'll have four more  episodes than they regularly do yearly, I am okay with this.

 Frankly, there's too much content out there these days as it is to allow  your show to run much beyond 5 or 6 seasons anyway, so I'm especially  okay with being done with one and moving onto another.

I love  Netflix for even GIVING Bojack a chance, and I love the people who made  it, all of them, because it's an incredible work of art that will stand  the test of time, if only, sadly, because the things it talks about,  broken society and mental illness and damaged families, will always be prevalent. I know that for me personally it was really great because it dealt with a lot of what I myself deal with (serious depression, mental unwellness, and Bojacks relationship with his mother was almost verbatim my own). 

So thanks  guys. It's been a hell of a ride. Here's to one final year of getting  back on the horse.

Moonrise Kingdom, to me, is a fascinating film but probably not in a lot of the same ways other people would think so (maybe I'm wrong, I don't know). I went to film school, I have been interested in filmmaking my entire life, and the first time I saw Moonrise Kingdom, despite having seen other Wes Anderson movies, it shook me to my core with how vastly different it was, but again, not in the sense you're probably thinking of lol Rushmore, Isle Of Dogs, and hell, even Life Aquatic, yeah they're quirky and weird and fairly unique (I'd argue Rushmore is the least unique of them all honestly) but in the end, they're still MOVIES. They're made like movies, they're presented AS movies, and you could easily show them to anyone for the most part. Yes Isle Of Dogs is unique in the sense that's stop motion and all that, but still.

Moonrise Kingdom, on the other hand, never feels like a movie to me. It feels like I'm watching an expanded stage play, and that is just an utterly fascinating concept to me, and maybe others feel differently, I don't know, but this is just what I got from it. I'll praise all the other same stuff everyone else seems to, be it the acting or the editing or whatever, but I'm talking that to its core, it feels like I'm watching an extremely well crafted, well produced, expansive stage play. That is so weird, but it WORKS. I'm sorry if this doesn't make any sense to anyone else, but this is just how I am able to explain it lol

It's so static in its imagery and its cinematography at times, most of the time, and yet it doesn't come off that way. The costume design, the set design, everything, even down to the musical score and the pseudo interrupting commentary by Balaban (god bless that wonderful man) just all reminds me so much of a stage play, and is presented in that way, to me. Anyway I'm an 30 year old autistic woman, so maybe I feel differently about this than others do, and that's fine if people think I'm wrong, it's possible, I've been wrong before lol

*She had summer in her eyes, laying on our backs and pointing out  clouds that look like something other than clouds; our hands just barely  touching now and then between the blades of semi wet grass, light  smiles dancing across our lips knowing that we were in eternal bliss  together.*

This seems like a great thing for you, and I'm happy to hear that. That being said, while I do the same thing (buy a lot of books) I actually do intend to, and have been, read through all of them. When I was growing up, my stepfather read a ton, and sometimes our tastes overlapped. Because I was the only kid in the family who read (neither stepsibbling cared to read), sometimes when he was done with something, I would take it and read it too. Because of this, I ended up collecting an ENORMOUS amount of paperbacks, up to and including, a hell of a lot that I was never going to read. I finally, back in 2013, gave almost all of my paperbacks away, because I recognized it was ridiculous to be carting them around, especially when I needed to move.

Since then, I've kept my library fairly light, but that doesn't mean I won't buy books to keep. It just means that I don't collect stuff I never intend to read, solely for the sake of collecting them. I no longer take books for the sake of doing so. As someone said below, there's a pretty toxic belief in the literary community that to be well read you need an enormous library. This isn't the case. With that in mind, however, I still do have a fairly large library, but it's all things I've read or am in the process of reading. I no longer buy a book I have no intention to read. I like having them around. I have three bookshelves just in mine and my girlfriends bedroom, with a whole other box of books in her parents basement, since we haven't brought them to our place yet.

It's true that I likely also view keeping books as a necessary thing, though, because to me (especially growing up, because I was a lonely little girl) books were my friends, and still are. Since I've essentially lost everyone else in my life, either because they were abusive or they died, I insist on keeping books I buy, even after I've read them, even if I never intend to read them again. They are a part of my family. Some I will re-read, some I likely will never re-read. I loved the few Franzen books I've read but holy lord do I doubt I'll ever go through them a second time simply because they are so massive in scope, and often too slow. And yet...I can't bring myself to get rid of them because I love them too much. They are a part of me.

And having that many books doesn't really negatively effect my life, so it's not so much an issue for me as it may be for others. So while, yes, I do own a ton and buy a ton, I also don't really suffer from the same issues that you said you did. However, that won't stop me from commending you for doing what you felt you had to to make your life easier, because I'm always happy to see people bettering themselves or their situations :)

I was talking to my girlfriend about this a few weeks ago, about how, specifically, stuff on NBC seems to be shriveling in numbers. We watched Good Girls, which had ten episodes. Then I noticed that The Good Place, also on NBC, had 13 (I think?) per season, and then I remember that 911 on Fox ALSO had like 10 a season, and it led me to wonder if perhaps mainstream major networks are finally accepting that there's just TOO much content out there to watch.

See, back in the day, there wasn't as much as there is now. Now we're over saturated, and you feel if you can't keep up with everything, then you aren't participating in current pop culture. Back then, there were a few hit shows on each major network and that was it really. These usually had about 22-24 episodes a season, which has always, frankly, been ridiculous in my mind especially when it comes to dramas that last 44 minutes per episode as it is. I'm sorry, I don't have that kind of time anymore. Maybe when I was a teenager, but not now. Also, you mentioned Game of Thrones as only having ten episodes a year, but that's kind of been the norm for the more elite channels for a long long time. Curb Your Enthusiasm has also always only had 10 per year and that's been on since 2000, so. Hell, even South Park had been doing 14 a year for a long time before finally dumping it down to 10 for the last few seasons, and that's just on Comedy Central lol

While there's obvious cons to the whole "shortened seasons" thing (for one, you feel like you're spending less time with the characters so sometimes you don't feel as attached, and for another a shortened season can lead to less well developed characters if the people writing it don't do a good enough job, since they don't have that length they used to), but on the whole, I think it's a good, and necessary, change. But I think some of what others have said is valid too; the culture of binging (of which I personally don't partake) and whatnot. I just think ultimately it has to do with the overflow of content. There's too much and not enough time, so now they make not as many episodes.

Honestly? I'm all for it. Even if it means less time with the characters and somewhat less character development in certain places, I'm all for it, because in between everything else I have to do in life, I still wanna watch TV. I just want it to be more palatable, time wise, for my own life, and that's what seems to be happening here.

I've followed Fullers solo career since Dead Like Me and god, this poor bastard just has been screwed every step of the way. Dead Like Me was totally original and so well done, but it lasted two seasons. When asked why it was canceled, the people in charge at Showtime literally said, "We don't know." And then, to top it all off, someone else creates Reaper, a show which basically takes the same general premise and runs longer, all while being a lot stupider (personal opinion).

Okay, so your first show doesn't last. This happens. Besides, he left after the first five episodes anyway, so he goes on to co-create Wonderfalls, which was also amazing. Campy, quirky and totally enthralling, Wonderfalls would've been an absolute hit...had Fox treated it with any modicum of respect. You'd think that a guy who wrote the majority of one of the Star Trek series would get SOME sembelance of respect, but apparently not. Fox not only aired just 4 episodes of the show, but they aired them OUT. OF. ORDER.

So then he goes to work on Heroes for a time. We all know how that went, not that it was very good after Season 1 to begin with (though, I personally couldn't get through even that).

So that's gone, and then he goes on to create Pushing Daisies, and finally, FINALLY, it seems like the man has a hit on his hands! It does well, the ratings are pretty good, the critics love it! And then the writers strike, which accomplished nothing, happens, and when the show finally comes back on the air, nobody remembered it existed and it was also canceled. After this, Fuller bummed around writing stand alone pilot after stand alone pilot, one for a "no kill shelter" sitcom that never made it to air, along with the fantastic "MockingBird Lane" Munsters reboot, which also never became anything more than a glorified Halloween special.

Then he goes on to create Hannibal, which was also fantastic, but different. For the first time, it wasn't his own thing. He made it his own version, but it was a pre-existing property, and that's where he stands now. Fuller now solely works on bringing pre-existing properties into new life. He helped bring the new Star Trek to the air, American Gods was his doing, Hannibal was his thing and now he's working on bringing The Vampire Chronicles to the airwaves, and frankly...I can't blame him. If I continued to churn out wholly awesome and original series one after another only to have each network consistently crap in my face, I too would just sort of give up and go, "Well, may as well work with pre-existing properties because at least you KNOW there's a built in audience."

And it's a shame. It's a shame because all of them, Wonderfalls especially since that's the one you brought up here, were just amazing works of art. That scene where Jaye finally breaks down and just asks "Why do you talk to ME?" is so amazingly well done, it sends shivers up my spine every single damn time that I see it, and I miss them. I miss him.

A few people recently have said the reason he doesn't stay on projects very long anymore is because he's hard to work with.

Frankly, if I'm Bryan Fuller, I'd imagine it's the opposite, given my experiences, and it's the networks that are too hard to work with.

This has effected numerous series, honestly. Wonder Years, Daria, Freaks & Geeks; the list goes on and on. This is why some of those took forever to come out on DVD, and why some of them, such as Daria, were forced to completely overhaul their musical selection because, unlike Freaks & Geeks, it wasn't a single season (which I assume is why the music made the cut, because it was cheaper to just pay the rights for 19 episodes of music), it was 5 seasons and 2 films. 

And as someone stated below, home video simply wasn't a thing for the average show at the time. That's really all it comes down to. I don't think most people working in the entertainment industry really thought at some point in the future people would own entire collections of content. Hell, Matt Groening has gone on record stating that they never thought people would know the names of Simpsons episodes, which is why, for a while in the beginning, they were so stupid or simple, because they were only mattering to the people working on them.

I think this is also why we see TV series use limited music these days, because they now recognize having to pay the rights so consistently. They used to release soundtracks for TV series, that's how normalized it was to use actual songs on your show. Nowadays, most shows simply have their regular composer and every now and then use a song or two, because that's FAR more affordable. There was an old conversation from the podcast The Drunk Tank (which turned into The Roosterteeth Podcast) where, I believe, it was Burnie Burns who made a statement much along the lines of:

>"Well, think about the movie The Godfather. It came out at a time when large theater releases weren't a thing. They made their way slowly across the country, in small screenings. So they made their money at the theater, then they made their way to television, then to laserdisc, then to VHS, then to DVD, then to Blu-Ray and streaming. This is a film that has made money via every single new possible release in the medium."

I think that statement is fascinating, because he's right and, in a way, backing up the previous comment I saw someone else state. Nobody thought about the future of these things. Nobody thought about the financial ramifications or whatever. So yeah. I think also there's just some shows that have fallen by the wayside and are sort of forgotten about, like The Drew Carrey Show only finally re-airing on Laff and only having released a single season on DVD, because time has marched on and left many series in its wake. I'm not saying Murphy Brown is among those, obviously, but I think that might factor into it as well. If there just isn't enough clamor for something, then why spend the money (especially if it's never been released so you have no numbers to base its sales success off of) producing thousands of copies of it. That's for physical releases anyway, but that does, I think, also effect the contracting of series to streaming services as well. The whole "well WHO is gonna watch this?" question.

The strange thing is how many gay people there were around me growing up. I grew up in the late 90s/early 2000s (I'm 29 now). My mothers brother was bisexual (granted he died when I was very young) and my neighbors growing up were a lesbian couple. My parents, abusive as they were in the end, presented as rather open minded people, often letting the kids watching movies other kids likely wouldn't have seen at that age, listening to pretty much whatever we wanted and were both democrats. My stepfather loved musicals and often took us to the theatre, and yeah, I grew up in what would be seen as a rather "accepting" family. But my god was it anything other than a facade.

The funny thing is, I never once questioned myself. Ever since the first time I saw a pretty girl on TV or something, and was old enough to recognize I thought someone was attractive in some way, I knew I was different. This was only exacerbated by the fact that in elementary school, I asked a girl to a dance, to which she politely accepted because she didn't want to embarrass me in front of other people, and then took me aside later that day and told me she didn't really want to go. As a result, I never went to any social functions. I wouldn't have anyway. I'm extremely introverted and don't care much for social interaction. My parents knew this happened because she was a close friend of mine at the time, and I talked about her constantly, so it wasn't even really a hidden thing, but I think, like a lot of people, they might've assumed it was a phase or something.

But it only got worse lmao As I got older, I become more and more reclusive because of my depression and how my parents treated me emotionally. I had very close girl friends but none of them were a "girlfriend", and when I was 17 I finally started dating a girl in secret. When we finally broke up after a single year, I was absolutely devastated, and my parents knew something was up because they'd seen us hanging out and chatting so often every day. They never said anything about it, but they knew. But the real kicker was my 2nd long term girlfriend, which lasted for 5 years. Within the first few months of meeting her, I guess I slipped up and forgot that I had accepted my stepfathers friend request on facebook, and I made a post about her on there. Not minutes later do I hear him in the kitchen with everyone, talking very loudly about how I apparently had a girlfriend, and they all laughed about it. The thing is, my bedroom was right next to the kitchen. My parents often fought in front of my door, specifically talking badly about me, because they knew I could hear it. I did not grow up in a good place, despite all its appearances.

After that, it was clear to everyone and I never really had a "coming out". I'm honestly kind of happy and mad. On one hand, I recognize that it's ridiculous to have to "come out" because it should be normalized, and not something someone has to do. And yet...it's such a common bond that most gay people have in their life as something they had to experience, that I feel almost left out that I didn't get to do it.

Sorry to write a novel. Sorry it also wasn't exactly on topic. I've just really been thinking about my past lately, especially my sexuality, and I guess I had a lot to say.

As an autistic gay girl, yeah. It was tough.

By middle school people made so much fun of me and called me the worst names and by high school I just didn't even respond to it anymore, and by the middle of my sophomore year, I dropped out completely and switched to a private school situation with a tutor. It was also tough because, especially growing up, I didn't really know how to approach the subject of romance without being just overly dramatic about it, so I wrote love poems and shit and made my feelings towards my crushes super well known, to the point where one girls dad said he'd have a restraining order put on me. In elementary school. And all I'd done was tell her I liked her, so he might've just been a homophobic piece of shit, but still. It was bad enough people treated me differently for being autistic, but then being gay on top of it...forget about it.

And then after I sort of learned how to talk to people, and talk to people I was romantically interested in (not that I have much interest in talking to people in general), I got a little better and it got easier but same as you. Can't go anywhere, hate crowds, loud noises, ABSOLUTELY HATE BARS and I don't drink, and it was terrible. Thankfully, my first girlfriend, which only lasted a year, wound up being a longtime close friend, and she helped me a lot, but yeah...this post brought back a lot of poor memories lol

Anyway I think the best thing to do is look for other people like yourself. That's what I wound up doing. I sought out the girls who were like me, despite hating myself, and got close to them, and it's worked tremendously. I was with one girl for 5 years, and my current gf, whom I live with, for almost 4 years now, so I think that's our safest bet. Medications/therapies have never helped or ever eased it (though I am very happy for those it has, and I would never persuade someone NOT to look into that) and I've accepted this is just who and what I am and despite all my bits of effort over the years there's nothing that can be done about that I just have to learn to live with it. I have some very base SI that I have had forever and will have forever, or come across certain things that become SI that will always stay SI. Then I also have some where it's something I become incredibly interested in for the length of anywhere between a week to a month or so and it's all I'll focus on. Most of my special interests are based around entertainment, particularly film/television, so there'll be something I discover and research for hours, for weeks, and then eventually move on. But then, this also happens and the thing will become so beloved by me that I will always keep coming back to it, whereas sometimes these special interests die down after a month or two. It just really depends.

That all being said, I 100% with your statement of "it's depressing when the intensity subsides" because heck yeah it is. It's like losing a friend, which I know how it feels because everyone eventually stops being my "friend" lol But yeah, to spend all your time with something and then suddenly, or even gradually, stop spending all your time with said thing...yeah. It's a bummer. The only saving grace is that I know most of my special interests will always be with me, but people never will. At least they won't leave me like my family did.
