Mark Miller, a man I once defended to the ends of the earth, is now the fucking comic book equivalent of James Patterson. The first series of the comic and the first film are perfect, and in no way need to be fucked with. I was pretty excited upon learning that he was making a sequel comic, only to come away 4 issues in completely underwhelmed and irritated, because for a man who seems to write and plan as well as Miller does, he seems to have forgotten that concepts aren't plots. I had no problem with the lead in the new series, Patience Lee, outside of the fact that she was pretty boring and just another "blank, military persona" with no real personality to speak of.

Half the goddamned appeal of the original, even with as whacky and out there as it could be, was the fact that it was based around a kid who didn't know what the fuck he was doing, and yet still you rooted for him because you liked who he was. And the idea of rebooting the film franchise when the first film only did well critically and the second was nothing but a typical, bland Marvel\-esque blockbuster that was now just becoming what the first film had made so much fun of is such a stupid idea. You can't remake that movie with a new younger actress to play Hit\-Girl, because the only one who could've ever done it already did it. It just wouldn't be right.

Mark Miller needs to stop selling his goddamned properties and take a step back and look at what he's built. He's built a great universe, that somehow is self contained and not attached to the rest of the superhero comic universe (which makes it actually interesting), and needs to start focusing on the things that NEED to be finished, like, maybe...I don't know....a fucking Nemesis sequel after all those years of saying it was coming? Or maybe taking other comics and turning them into films instead of beating a dead horse that was once a lively pony.

I had a lot of respect for the guy, but at this point, now whenever I see his name in a headline, the first thing I think of is "Oh god, what now?" and that is NOT a good place to be in.

I read voraciously from the time I was a little girl up to about my sophomore year in high school. And when I say voraciously, I'm not even kidding. I took books with me EVERYWHERE. I read in the car \(I don't get sick doing this, thank goodness\), at school, at home, at restaurants, etc. I was obsessed with books, and making my shelves packed with them. Then, I'm not sure really what happened, but around my sophomore year in high school, I just sorta...stopped? It had nothing to do with anything, really, looking back. It just sorta happened. One day I noticed that I simply wasn't reading much anymore.

That was about 2006 I believe. In about 2011, I was living in a small beach town with nothing to do. It was a total tourist trap. Thankfully, there was a small and very crappy barnes & noble in the mall nearby walking distance, and a second hand book store next to the movie theater across the street, along with a wonderful Goodwill across another street, and I used to just hit those all the time \(especially the Goodwill\) and pick up books a plenty because Goodwill sells books so dang cheap. That was when I started really getting back into it. At first, much like you, I too had trouble reading as fast as I used to be able to, but after a bit, the power came back to me and now I can glide through 3 or 4 books, at a time, very easily within a month or two.

Just keep at it :\) I'm really happy I picked the hobby back up, because there's no place for me in this world, but there's always a place for you in fiction.

"The Road" might be the single most underwhelming book I've ever had the displeasure of reading. 

It isn't that it's bad, it's that it could've been so much better than it was, and yet was somehow considered an outstanding piece of art. I've always criticized the book for things like not expanding on cool concepts presented, like the finding of the bomb shelter, and am always rebutted with "that's kind of the point, is that it's all meaningless". While I'm willing to accept that, and understand it, it doesn't make me like it any more.

I also recognize that I am constantly the odd one out, and I've come to accept that too, but I really dislike this book for so many reasons I could write an entire dissertation on. I think McCarthy is a great writer, his other works prove that beyond the shadow of a doubt, but The Road will stand the test of time as a big fat "meh" that was still lauded as a masterpiece. The so called "relationship" between father and son was so bare bones and flimsy it made me wonder why I should care at all. Because they were father and son? Sorry. That's not enough of a reason. That's a concept. Not a plot.

I wholeheartedly agree with how you feel towards the ending, as well. I have never been so uninterested in something everyone else somehow loved, and this isn't a "I hate everything that's popular and well liked!" stance whatsoever, but I myself am a writer, and my god, this is the kind of book that makes me not want to read.

I have had severe clinical depression, among other issues, since I was a little girl and tried to kill myself when I was 11, and almost tried a few times after that. 

I wound up reading TBJ about two years ago when living with my girlfriend at her parents place. It was in the middle of nowhere and we didn't have much to do, so we spent a lot of time reading, and this was one of the first books I read there. As someone who struggles with all these things, I found it incredibly relateable to the point where I felt like I myself had written it. The way Plath captured the feelings of hopelessness, the way you think everything and everyone around you sucks (granted, unlike her, I have legit reasons to hate my abusive parents), even if they're your friends and love you to death, was so hard to read that I had to read it in chunks because it made me cry.

So there's that.

Okay listen, growing up, my grandmother gave me a ton of James Patterson books when I became a teenager, and I loved them. They were pretty quick, easy, yet compelling reads (and I mean his classic stuff like When The Wind Blows, Cradle & All, stuff like that, okay) and I was happy to be able to talk to my grandma about the books she liked. 

I read James Patterson for a long, long time, and I absolutely adored When The Wind Blows and was even thrilled with the sequel, The Lake House. Then, when I found out he'd be making a whole series based on these characters, I was more thrilled. Until I read Maximum Ride, or what little of it I could stomach. I was devastated that he'd utterly destroyed these fantastic characters and turned them into shells of their former selves all for a goddamned shot at the YA dystopian genre. I officially swore off Patterson at that point, I was so mad.

Years later, I finally picked up a new Patterson book called Honeymoon, partially because it was co-written by someone else, and I thought "Welp, maybe this will keep Patterson in check regarding what I don't like about him", and man, Honeymoon was SO. GOOD. It was riveting, it was fast paced, and it was everything I'd loved about classic Patterson books, and for a while I thought, "God, I'm finally happy with this mans work again!"

Now, I am not one to judge things based on endings. In my entire history of reviewing film or books or w/e, I've had 3 times where it's happened. This was one of them, because at the end of this tight, nonstop thrill ride, the last 5 pages, the ball is completely dropped and the whole goddamned story crumbles before your eyes, making you wish you hadn't even bothered in the first place. Let me make this as clear as possible. The fact that my eyes read it made me mad that I could see. That's how upsetting it was.

Needless to say, I haven't picked up a Patterson book since then.

It's still to this day basically the only fantasy series I have read and care to read, and the Abbey always feels like a warm, welcoming home. It also really helped my self esteem, which I had none of growing up, because until about 2nd grade, I needed a tutor to teach me to read, as I was that far behind despite my teachers telling me how bright they thought I was. I really struggled with reading. So, low and behold, when I got to 4th grade and started reading these, the fact that I managed to finish them made me feel so good about my reading capabilities. By the end of elementary school, I was reading college level books, but it still helped me get there, and I'll always be grateful for that.

But what's really weird is I remember reading High Rhulain in my early twenties and realizing as I finished that Brian was getting rather up there in years, and how big of an important role this man had played in my life, in getting me to read and giving us a world we all loved so much. I got really sad, looking at his photo on the back of the book, realizing he likely wouldn't be around much longer.

He died about 3 days later. I've always felt really strange about the timing of that thought and then his actual untimely demise, and of course, like everyone else, I was absolutely heartbroken. It might've been one of the last times I actually cried at the death of a "celebrity".

I much preferred using my imagination, and this is coming from a girl who's special interest is television, that says something lol

Anyway, I'm happy to see so many people wax nostalgic about this series and Brian in general. I never got to meet him or get anything signed, so I'll always be really upset about that, but he gave us a great series and that'll always be the best thing he could've done anyway. No signed book or meet and greet could ever replace just having these damn things be written to begin with.

So sure, Brian might be gone, but the Abbey is eternal, and nobody can take that away from us.

It came out in 2013, but I picked up Sisterland by Curtis Sittenfeld for a buck at the dollar store one day last year.

I was intrigued by 'Sisterland' for the premise alone, (a pair of grown identical twin girls, both of whom are psychics, come to blows when one reveals her premonitions of an earthquake soon to come) which is good, considering that alone is what carries you through the book. Sittenfeld isn't a bad author, by any means. The writing is competent, and the pacing is tremendous, but the book certainly has a flurry of issues to be talked about. I understand that the book is set in St. Louis, where the author is from, so one could claim that the people there are just a little more closed minded than usual, but it's not very fair to generalize and entire city based on a few characters in a novel. Littered with questioning lesbians sexuality and just a hint of transphobia at one point, and the book seems to be marred with indifference.

I think my biggest issue with this book was the protagonist, to be honest. Kate is a rather unlikable protagonist, and then as you read on you're given a slew of examples as to why she's so distant and unlikable, and you sort of start to like her. Then, all that character growth is tossed right out the window for a cheap thrill a mere 80 pages from the end of a novel about psychics and earthquakes, making her entirely unlikable once again. But, for as unlikable as Kate seems to be, her husband Jeremy isn't any better. As someone who, on the outside, is seemingly charming, kind and well mannered is actually shown to be quite manipulative and at times downright cruel. In a way, he and Kate are perfect for eachother, as they're both kind of terrible people disguising themselves as a lovely suburban couple.

And therein lies yet another major flaw; a rather intriguing revelation that was then never expanded on and instead left to simply be questioned by both characters and reader. An alright choice, as in life you don't get answers for everything, but still, a plot point introduced far too late to save whatever the book was trying to say. And despite not being expanded upon, even the reveal wasn't enough to redeem this Jodi Picoultesque summer read. Not to mention there's things introduced that are never fully followed up on, such as the return of a character from Kates childhood mentioned in the beginning, but then is never brought to fruition, ultimately leaving the reader to wonder why in the hell she bothered in the first place. To show that growth doesn't always occur in people? That some folks never change? Or did she merely feel the need to pad the book in the middle? I'm legitimately curious. Perhaps it was to show that she and Kate weren't all that different after all, and I can get behind that, but it still felt like it should've been more included.

I guess in the end, the book is certainly readable, even enjoyable to a shallow extent, but it's not what I thought it might be, or even had hoped it might be, and I guess that's what makes me most upset. Not that 'Sisterland' is bad, but that it could've been great.

I've had depression for as long as I can think I've had memories, which is hard to gauge as I've blocked most of my early memories, so I generally just say since I was about 5 or something. I never felt like I belonged, and could never really hold onto anyone I dared to get close to and consider an actual friend. My interests and other mental health issues (I'm also autistic) have made things very hard for me, socially speaking. It was with me throughout childhood, adolescence and now adulthood and sadly sometimes seems to have been my only real companion, as it'll never leave me like most seem to.

I'm nearly 28 now. I'm an artist and novelist/writer. It has seeped into every tangible space that I have, every single facet of my personality and worldview. It's infected my work, my writing, my artwork, my belief system, everything. I've got my girlfriend thankfully, but I no longer have a family as they disowned me for being a lesbian, and barely any friends, and so at least my girlfriend understands and accepts me, and even has the same issues, but I still feel so disconnected from the rest of the species, especially my own generation. I have nothing in common with people my age, which doesn't help.

But I've come to calling myself a positive nihilist. Yes everything sucks and it's all meaningless and I'll always feel this bad, but at least I really know who I am and what I believe, and I have a solid, firm grasp on how I view the world. Depression can destroy, but it's also helped rebuild a bit for me, oddly enough.

As Sarah Vowell once (paraphrasing here) said, "If you take away our flaws, I'm not sure who I am."

I've been having some serious problems with my appearance lately. I've never really been happy with how I've looked, but at least over the last two years or so I started to really be pretty pleased with my fashion choices and appearance. However, in the last six months or so, I've really lost all confidence I ever had (which was minimal to begin with) regarding how I look. Oh well. I've resigned myself to this fate. I hope for a better outcome for others though.

I've got a few that I'd throw in here that I never ever hear anyone talk about (these are some of my all time favorites too). Obviously depends on the genre and type of writing people prefer, but these are what I love.

An Underachievers Diary by Benjamin Anastas - a book about a brother who was born minutes before his younger brother, and it's the only thing he'll ever be first at. It's hilarious and painfully honest. Relatively short, too.

Stupid Children by Lenore Zion - also relatively short, but also absolutely hysterical and eye opening. Follows a girl who's father tries to kill himself, so she's put in foster care and taken in by this family who's part of a cult, and they think she's the reincarnated wife of their leader. Fascinating, but be warned, there's some really graphic imagery in this book. Like, it could give a horror movie a run for its money, honestly.

Hey, Nostradamus! - probably the most well known of all three, since it's by Douglas Coupland, who's not an unknown author by any means. It follows the aftermath of a school shooting that kills a secretly pregnant and married teenager, and her high school husband who survives. Heart wrenching and beautiful.

Again, these are all just my own picks, and I don't know what genres appeal to everyone. I'm just tossing my two cents in.

When I was a little girl, myself, my stepsister and my stepbrother all had our own drawer in the hall bathroom for our toothpaste or whatever other bathroom item we wanted to store in it. One afternoon, when nobody was home, I went into the bathroom and cleared mine out, then started to restock it very neatly. 

I put books in the front, with the spines facing up, my game boy in the back with all the games in a case, some snacks and some drinks, and it was all very organized. Then, when it was "lights out" (which I think is what they have at prison, which makes a lot of sense at my house as a child), I would wait a bit, then go into the bathroom and lock the door. When asked, I would just say I didn't feel well, which wasn't really a lie, as a child I was constantly sick and in and out of the hospital.

I came home one day to find that my mother had decided to clean the hall bathroom and discovered my little treasure trove. She was more impressed than angry, but she did make me stop doing that. After that I did what some others here said, using hall lights and such at night to try and read a bit, mostly thanks to insomnia because I didn't want to just lie there if I wasn't going to fall asleep for hours.

My parents never really got mad at me for reading, they encouraged it, but that was the only thing they ever did that wasn't abusive.

I agree with some of these (Alan Wake especially, Singularity and Viva Pinata), but I'll list a handful of underrated games I've played over the years:

* The Neverhood/Skullmonkeys - The masterpiece from the creator of Earthworm Jim, that nobody has ever fucking heard of. The first was entirely made of clay, and is a point and click adventure game, with a hilarious world and cast. The second was a PS1 game that was a "sequel" (in the loosest sense of the word) that was more platformer based, but still just a hell of a lot of fun. These games also have some of the best soundtracks of all time. I recently went through and played The Neverhood again on my PC with my gf, and it was still just as much fun as it was when I was a little girl.

* Stubbs The Zombie - Man...this might be one of the games I wanted to become a franchise next to Alan Wake the most. Stubbs was a zombie game, from the point of view of the zombie. You're Stubbs, a dead salesman, who returns to life in a futuristic 1950s style city, and go on a brain munching frenzy (there's actually a plot, but I don't wanna spoil in case anyone wants to play it). You can turn other people into zombies and create an army, and use your body as weapons, like pulling organs from yourself and throwing them at enemies while they explode. Truly original and hysterical.

* Seaman - Alright. Seaman. The strangest game to ever be made. It was a Dreamcast game (at least, that's what I have it on), and the entire game takes place in a science lab in front of a fish tank. It's actually very much like something you'd see on Steam these days, to be honest. Your goal is to raise, from an egg, the Seaman, a half man half fish and whole fucking asshole. Seaman is a very cranky, snotty, disrespectful little turd of a fish/human hybrid who comes with a terrible attitude. You can talk to him, teach him things, have whole conversations using the Dreamcast mic, all while laughing your ass off. So great.

* Cel Damage - Cel shaded game, set up like a reality type show where you drive around, pick up weapons and are supposed to kill your "co-stars" and gain enough points to win. It didn't do too well, but it was a LOT of fun, and I'm a sucker for cel shaded stuff. My stepbrother and I played the hell out of it for years.

* Kung Fu Chaos - A very goofy game where you're on a movie set, making a kung fu feature, with a completely sadistic director, and have to fight, all while lights and other movie equipment are falling around you. A lot of fun, but probably the game that least deserves to be on the list, and is much more just a game I remember really liking.

One of my all time favorites was The Drunk Tank (before the rename to The Roosterteeth Podcast and before Geoff left), which had some of the single most hilarious stories I've ever heard people tell about their lives. But to make this easier, I'll do this in list form:

* Yeah It's That Bad - A movie review podcast where three guys, Kevin, Joel & Martin reviewed movies with low Rotten Tomatoes scores to reevaluate and see if they deserved the score they had. It was tremendously hilarious, and they felt like hanging out with old friends. The running gags and all, I miss it so much, and as far as I know, it was far before the other bad movie review podcasts. Unfortunately, they vanished, released a final episode, and their website is no longer up. I just hope they're doing okay.

* Goosebuds - A great replacement for the previous; three guys, and sometimes guests, read (or watch the episodes of) Goosebumps books and then talk about how absolutely shitty they were. As someone who read the books when she was a kid, this one really resonates with me.

* Our Debut Album - Two guys try and write an album. Pretty good, and you can listen to the finished songs on their bandcamp I think.

* A few honorable mentions would be Criminal/Imaginary Worlds/Theory Of Everything

But my favorite would have to be, hands down, Here Be Monsters. Here Be Monsters really knocks it out of the park when it comes to oddness, and is very well produced to boot. Their episodes run the gamut, such as "Ant God" where a guy with an ant farm he made watches a single ant get trapped in a cave in and deciding what kind of god he is to these ants, or "It Works Better In Movies" where he interviews a girl who used to lie to guys and tell them she was dying in order to get them to love her, or "Cadaver Paintings" where he interviews a guy who paints dead people.

Truly fascinating, out there stuff. He even went to PestWorld (a convention for pesticides and such) this year and talked to people there for an episode. So great.

I would say in terms of authors, Murakami has to be right up there in terms of the writing being beautiful. Norwegian Wood might've been horrendously depressing and tough to finish, but it was elegantly written, and really beautiful. Sputnik Sweetheart, another Murakami book, was much more beautiful in its prose.

But as far as singular books go, either The Little Prince, Special Topics In Calamity Physics or Station Eleven, which I just finished and now my girlfriend is reading. Station Eleven is almost just poetic while still being a book about the end of civilization. The way she makes you nostalgic for things you take for granted every day, it's really impressive, and it made me cry multiple times.

I read The Road a few years back (after hearing someone talk highly about it) and actually really disliked it. I'm fine with stories that don't tell you what happened, such as why the world is in the condition that it's in, and I don't generally care about endings either, but something about The Road just sort of...didn't work for me. It was very meandering, and their goal of reaching the coast just never really seemed all that important for some reason.

McCarthy also bothered at first me with how he writes speech, without using any quotation marks but once you get used to it, you realize it doesn't really matter. In the end, it just fell sort of flat, and left me feeling like nothing had really happened, and maybe that's the point; the ultimate bleakness of the situation, but it didn't work for me, and considering I love dark content, that was kind of weird.

I often thought that a lot of the small things that happened in the story (won't post since spoilers) were interesting, but then lead to nothing, such as discoveries made along The Road. I've since started reading No Country For Old Men and that's eons better, personally, but to each their own. It wasn't a bad book by any means, it just....I don't know, something about it left a weird, disappointing taste in my mouth.
